newsitem.title: UK: Strong UK-Asia air cargo market faces uncertainty.
newsitem.headline: Strong UK-Asia air cargo market faces uncertainty.

text.p: UK airline cargo managers focusing on London-Far East routes are generally reporting healthy, steady market conditions but some fear their industry faces an uncertain period, a Reuters survey shows.
Carriers serving Japan, which operates on a March-April financial year basis, noted business had been boosted by end 1996-97 purchases by importers anxious to spend their allocated budgets.

Imminent uncertainty may be caused by the adverse effect of the recent ever-strengthening sterling, the onset of Japan's new fiscal year and its accompanying budgetary restraints, and marketplace indecision surrounding Britain's May 1 general election.
"Our ex-UK cargo volumes to Singapore and Australia are up on this time last year and both markets are pretty stable," said Barry Gibson, Singapore Airlines' SIAL.S UK cargo manager.

"But the strength of sterling is at last having an effect on the overseas purchases of British goods. Couple that with the upcoming election and I foresee a tough summer, perhaps a tough year, ahead," he added.
Tony Edwards, Japan Airlines' UK cargo sales manager, said he was currently experiencing an end of fiscal year/end-first quarter 1997 boom period.
"March is always good for us and this year it has been excellent, with all our flights full and our staff being kept very busy indeed," he said.

"The effect of the strong pound is showing signs of having an (adverse) effect on Japanese import orders. And we also have to take into consideration the increase to five from three percent on April 1 of Japan's consumption tax."
Edwards declined to forecast his ex-UK cargo prospects for the rest of this year. JAL is waiting until next month before deciding on following many other carriers with an ex-UK cargo rate rise.
John O'Shea, All Nippon Airways' assistant UK cargo manager, said virtually all of ANA's UK-Japan freight capacity was presently flying full.
But he conceded that the strength of sterling against the yen, and the consumption tax rise, "could have a possible downward effect on our business."
Thai Airways International's UK cargo manager Mike Miller said March was always one of his strongest months and this year was no exception.
"However, our industry does not really feel the brunt of currency fluctuations until many months after they happen," he said.
"We are still shipping out goods ordered some time ago and so we may yet feel the impact of the rise in sterling's value against Asian currencies," he added.

Dubai government-owned Emirates' UK cargo manager Ray Dissan said although there was generally a three-month 'cycle' between orders being placed and shipments moved, his business had not suffered during when sterling soared.
"So now sterling has declined against the dirham, I don't expect the value of currencies to have much of an effect our business," he said.

Air cargo trading ex-UK has been buoyant over recent weeks to most south east Asian destinations, although the average rate to Singapore has declined by five pence to 1.19 stg per kg for a 100 kg shipment.
Industry sources said this is mainly due to increased competition from transhipment carriers to the three direct airlines serving the route - SIA, British Airways and Qantas.
About 40 percent of Thai International's ex-UK cargo is bound for Thailand and the remainder for Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia and other Asian points.
"All are pretty strong markets at present," Thai's Miller said.

Because of limited cargo capacity available on Thai's passenger flights ex-London, Miller is looking forward to the March 31 introduction of a third direct weekly Paris-Bangkok Boeing 747F flight on a joint basis with Air France.
The other two frequencies are flown by Air France aircraft, but this service will be operated by Thai's only 747 freighter.

"Most of what we carry from the UK is consolidated cargo," said Miller who will be boosting trucking of heavier shipments to connect with the ex-Paris and twice-weekly Frankfurt-Bangkok 747F services operated in conjunction with Lufthansa.
Nina Sturrock, UK cargo executive with Garuda, described as "pretty good" the state of its existing twice weekly MD-11 London Gatwick-Jakarta.

Like Miller, she is also eagerly anticipating extra new capacity through a new ex-London cargo weekly MD-11 servikce with an 18 tonnes capacity starting March 20 which will call at the Indonesian island of Batam, 20km off the coast of Singapore before continuing on to Denpasar (Bali).
Batam, whose Hang Nadim airport the Indonesian government has said will become an air cargo hub, offers "good, interesting and hopefully lucrative" ex-UK airfreight potential, she added.
Keith O'Callaghan, UK cargo manager of Philippine Airlines (PAL), said business is slightly down on last year, but could not specify why.
"But the London-Manila cargo market is nevertheless still very buoyant," he noted.
PAL's three-times-weekly Heathrow-Manila A340-200 passenger flights, can only carry 13 tonnes of cargo on the route when there is a full passenger load.

Although the date has been put back to July from May 4, he welcomed the introduction of a fourth weekly A340-200 flight on the route. The frequency is likely to be increased to five or six a week by end-1997.
"I don't think we'll have much trouble filling up the extra cargo capacity," he said
From the UK to eastern Asia, Thai's Miller said air cargo business to Hong Kong and especially to Japan and Korea was currently doing well.
JAL's Tony Edwards said that the most common types of UK-Japan airfreight -- computer shipments, pharmaceuticals, chemicals and cosmetics -- had lately been joined by increasing volumes of livestock.

Apart from the carrier's normal three weekly Heathrow-Tokyo 60-90 tonne capacity 747F services, an extra freighter flight had been operated on March 2 carrying horses for breeding and racing and another, earmarked for general freight, is scheduled for March 24.
"Additionally, we have just finished transporting 10 tonnes of breeding pigs, each weighing about 100 kg, bound for Japanese farms. Livestock is becoming a good sideline business for us," he added.
The average UK-Australia rate has steadily declined over the past month, to 2.08 stg per kg/100 kg from 2.18 stg in mid-February due to reduced demand for capacity, inspiring price cutting.
For 1,000 kg, certain carriers are achieving up to 1.60 stg per kg, but rates go down to the 90 pence level.

"Fifty percent of our ex-UK business is bound for Australia and New Zealand and although the state of this market is still reasonably good, there has been some considerable undercutting going on," said Garuda's Sturrock.

PAL's O'Callaghan also said he had noticed a wave of rate discounting on the London-Australia route, which accounts for 55-60 percent of his business, although he stressed that "we haven't got to that stage".
"It's all a question of over-capacity. The cake has got smaller and the amount of cargo space available has grown. This market is certainly not as buoyant as it was not so long ago," he added.

But Thai International's Miller said ex-UK, both the Australian and New Zealand air cargo markets were holding firm. "They are not falling away...there is no lack of interest," he said, adding that he was increasing hiOs rates to Sydney -- as well as to most Asian destinations -- by five percent from April 1.
Emirates' Ray Dissan said there was a lot more capacity available ex-London to Sydney, forcing downward pressure on rates, than to Melbourne, the only Australian destination his airline serves.
"In the last few months, our volumes to Melbourne have gone up and our yields have remained constant," he stated.
Only 15 percent of Emirates' UK-generated cargo for the Middle East is destined for home base Dubai, he added, with most of the remainder continuing on to Abu Dhabi, Doha, Muscat and Saudi Arabia.
"While over the past week we have been full up, our business to this region so far this calendar year has been up and down like a yo-yo. There has been no pattern...it is very strange," said Dissan.

"I think the close proximity of Christmas, Ramadan and Chinese New Year, all rapidly following one another, had a weird effect on trade. That, coupled with the strong pound for most of 1997 to date, has resulted in it being a strange year all round so far," he said.

There are between 15 and 20 carriers flying from the UK to the Indian subcontinent on various routeings. To the biggest market India, where the fiercest rivalry exists, these include Air India, BA, Air Canada, Lufthansa, Air France, Kuwait Airways, Royal Jordanian and Gulf Air.

"Competition has increased a hell of a lot on the route over recent years. But our business remains quite healthy, comprising FAK (freight-of-all-kinds) shipments including a lot of compter parts, machinery and aircraft parts," said an Air India air cargo source in London.
Air-India's ex-UK airfreight capacity has been severely curtailed over the past year, he added.
"Most of our 747 passenger flights from London originate in the U.S. and they get preferential treatment with regard to cargo space," he said.
"We have two weekly ex-UK 747 originators and share the 12-15 tonnes capacity available on each of these with our Paris office," he added.

Last year, the source said Air India Cargo UK was able to share allocations with New York, obtain space on three weekly Toronto-London-India flights and also had its own weekly 747 freighter operation ex-London.

"That's not the case any more, alas. We have no problem in filling up the restricted space we now have," he said, explaining that this would enable the carrier to raise its ex-UK cargo rates by five to eight percent from April 1.
With the average London-Bombay per kg/100 kg rate slightly up to 0.73 stg, per kg rates for 1,000 kg shipments on the route can be obtained from 40 to 50 pence upwards.
